steps.caption: Advance Variation after 5.Be2, Black to move. White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain. Study who can attack what before you read on.

claims.statement: The pawn on d4 is the base of White's chain: it defends e5 and no pawn defends it.
The pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6.
d6 is a hole in Black's camp: no black pawn can ever defend it.

steps.prompt: Black to move. Which pawn move would attack d4, the base of the chain? And which would attack e5, its head? Pick before you read on.

steps.text:
**A chain is attacked at its base.** The pawn on d4 defends e5, and nothing defends d4. Remove d4 and e5 has lost its support. So Black's main lever is the c-pawn: ...c5 hits d4. The other lever, ...f6, hits e5, which d4 already defends.
Both are *conditions*, not laws. [H] My hypothesis: the base is the usual target because it is the one chain pawn that no pawn defends.

steps.caption: Lever one: ...c5, part one. Step through how the base d4 gets attacked twice.

line.say: The pawn now attacks d4, the base of the chain. White has to decide how to meet it.
White adds a defender to d4 and develops a bishop in the same move.
A knight joins the pawn, so the base is attacked twice.

claims.statement: After ...c5 a black pawn attacks d4.
After ...Nc6 White's queen, knight and bishop defend d4.
After ...Nc6 two black men attack d4: the c5 pawn and the knight.

steps.caption: Part two: White keeps d4 defended and Black trades. See what the trade leaves.

line.say: White castles and keeps d4 defended three times against two attackers.
Black captures. The tension on d4 is over, and the c-file is half-open for Black: a rook there would aim at c2.
White recaptures with the knight, which now stands in the centre.

claims.statement: At the end Black has no pawn on the c-file and White none on the d-file.

steps.text: **What the trade leaves.** Black has no pawn on the c-file, so the file is half-open and a black rook can use it. White has no pawn on the d-file, so a white rook can use that one. The tension on d4 decided which files open; that is the practical meaning of a lever. The next exercise asks you to pick the lever yourself.

steps.caption: Lever two: ...f6. Same structure, but Black's knights are already on d7 and e7 and White has castled. Black plays ...f6.

line.say: The f-pawn now attacks e5, the head of the chain. Is this the right moment? The next exercise decides.

claims.statement: After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.
One white pawn, the pawn on d4, already defends e5.

steps.text:
**One position, one test.** In the position above the engine's top move is not ...f6: the lever is at least 85 centipawns behind the best move (depth 16) [V]. [H] My guess: d4 already defends e5, so White takes on f6 and the e-file opens while Black's king is still on e8. Untested.
**A question to try, not a rule:** what defends the pawn I am about to hit? We showed no position where ...f6 works, so test it yourself.

steps.caption: White to move after 5...c5. The base d4 is attacked once and defended twice. Think about what White wants before the next exercise.

claims.statement: One black pawn attacks d4.
Two white pieces defend d4: queen and knight.

steps.text: **White's job.** Keep the base defended, and do not release the tension too early: the capture dxc5 is at least 50 centipawns below the best moves here (depth 16) [V]. White's c-pawn can hit d5, but two pawns defend d5, so it is a head, not a base, and c4 is not the usual plan. [I] The chain gives White space, so White rarely needs to hurry.

steps.caption: White's usual plans here are Nbd2, c3 and a4. The pawn lever c4 is a rare try: it hits d5, which two pawns defend, so it is not aimed at a base.

line.say: The knight comes out; this is the most common move in the master set (106 games; c3 38, Nh4 25, a4 21).

claims.statement: Two black pawns (c6 and e6) defend d5.
After c4 a white pawn attacks d5.

steps.text: **Our master counts.** In this position our master set (329,379 games, both players 2,500+) lists 1,896 games. Black played the knight to e7 in 751, the other knight to d7 in 497 and the c-pawn to c5 in 493. After that pawn move White put the bishop on e3 in 352, castled in 83 and played c3 in 55. These are results of games, not evaluations.

steps.prompt: The engine's first choice here is ...c5, yet ...Ne7 and ...Nd7 were each played more often. What does that show?

steps.text: **No chain, a different map.** After the exchange on d5 each side has lost a central pawn: White has no e-pawn, Black no c-pawn. That gives White a half-open e-file, Black a half-open c-file, and each side a pawn majority on one wing. A majority is a plan; the question is when its lever is sound.

steps.caption: Exchange Variation, part one: White develops and protects d4.

line.say: White develops with a bishop aimed at the kingside.
Black adds a second attacker to d4.
The pawn defends d4 and leaves the queen's diagonal free.

steps.caption: Part two: Black develops, White's bishop gets out. Now read the pawns.

line.say: Black develops and watches the centre.
White develops the bishop outside the pawns before ...e6 can shut it.

claims.statement: White has no pawn on the e-file (half-open for White); Black has none on the c-file (half-open for Black).
White has four pawns on the queenside (files a to d).
Black has three pawns on the queenside.
White has three pawns on the kingside (files e to h).
Black has four pawns on the kingside.

steps.caption: Black's lever: ...e5, part one. Black offers to trade the dark-squared bishops.

line.say: The pawn supports d5 and opens a square for the bishop.
White develops and defends d4 again.
Black offers a trade of the dark-squared bishops.

steps.caption: Part two: the bishop that watched e5 is traded off.

line.say: White accepts. The bishop that watched e5 is gone.
The queen recaptures and eyes the kingside.
White castles. Black can wait.

claims.statement: After the trade White's bishop is no longer on f4.
Black's dark-squared bishop has left f8.

steps.caption: Part three: both sides castle and the lever comes.

line.say: Black castles too. Both kings are safe.
White develops the last minor piece and defends the centre.
Black's kingside majority steps forward: the pawn attacks d4.

claims.statement: After ...e5 a black pawn attacks d4.

steps.text:
**The conditions.** The three positions differ in one feature each. In the working one Black has castled. In the failing one the king and rook are back on e8 and h8, and ...e5 is at least 300 centipawns worse [V]. In the third only the a-pawn moved, and it changes nothing. [H] Hypothesis: opening the e-file is risky while your king is still on it.
Two rule checks follow.

**What a majority is for.** Four pawns against three on one wing: if the pawns there are traded one for one, a white pawn is left with no black pawn in front of it or beside it. That is a passed pawn, the long-term point of a majority [I]. The next question is whether it is time to push.

steps.caption: The Panov attack, part one: White strikes at d5 at once.

line.say: White strikes at d5 at once instead of developing.
Black develops and adds a second attacker to d5.
White adds a second attacker as well.

steps.caption: Part two: both sides develop and d5 is defended.

line.say: The pawn defends d5 and prepares the bishop's route.
White develops and defends d4.
Black prepares to castle.

steps.caption: Part three: the pawn exchange changes the structure. Read the result.

line.say: White captures. This pawn exchange changes the structure.
The knight recaptures and stands on d5.
White's bishop eyes the kingside and the d4 pawn is left alone.

claims.statement: White's d4 pawn is isolated: no white pawn stands on the c-file or the e-file.
d5 is an outpost for Black: a pawn defends it, no white pawn can attack it, and a black knight stands on it.

steps.text: **Our master counts, Exchange.** After the exchange on d5 our master set lists 1,683 games. White developed the bishop to d3 in 1,040, played the c-pawn to c4 in 379, the knight to f3 in 189 and the c-pawn to c3 in 56. After the c4 push Black developed a knight to f6 in 488 of 501. Counts show what was chosen, not what is best.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- A chain is attacked at its base.
- Before a lever, ask what defends the target, then test the idea.
- Advance: ...c5 first; in the one position we tested ...f6 was clearly worse, so check before you trust it.
- Exchange: each side has a wing majority; ...e5 needs the king castled and the pieces ready.
**Self-check:** did you say when it works, when it fails, one example, one mistake?
